questions.stem: The Little Desert dispute of 1969–70 in Victoria began when the state government planned to:
options: use the Little Desert as a weapons range
subdivide the Little Desert into new farms
flood the Little Desert for an irrigation dam
lease the Little Desert for uranium mining
questions.explanation: The Minister for Lands, Sir William McDonald, proposed clearing and subdividing the area for farming. Conservationists, scientists and rural residents campaigned against the scheme, which was dropped.

questions.stem: What was a lasting outcome of the Little Desert campaign?
options: Australia's first green political party was formed in western Victoria
Victoria set up the Land Conservation Council to assess the use of public land
The Little Desert was cleared for farms after the campaign was defeated
The Commonwealth took over control of all Victoria's public land and its national parks
questions.explanation: The dispute pushed the Bolte government to create the Land Conservation Council in 1970, giving public land decisions a scientific, consultative basis. Australia's first green party, the United Tasmania Group, formed in Tasmania in 1972.

questions.stem: Lake Pedder in south-west Tasmania was flooded in 1972 as part of:
options: a new water supply for the city of Hobart
a dam built to stop floods in Launceston
a Hydro-Electric Commission power scheme
an irrigation scheme for Tasmanian orchards
questions.explanation: The Hydro-Electric Commission's Middle Gordon scheme drowned the lake and its pink quartzite beach despite a national campaign. The loss became a rallying point for later campaigns, above all the Franklin.

questions.stem: The campaign to save Lake Pedder led in 1972 to the formation of:
options: the Nuclear Disarmament Party, which won a Senate seat for Tasmania
the United Tasmania Group, often called the world's first green party
the Australian Conservation Foundation, Australia's first national green group
the Australian Greens as a national party contesting federal elections
questions.explanation: The United Tasmania Group was formed in Hobart in 1972 to contest the state election on environmental issues. The Australian Conservation Foundation dates from the mid-1960s, the national Greens from 1992 and the Nuclear Disarmament Party from 1984.

questions.stem: The 'green bans' of the early 1970s were imposed by:
options: the Australian Conservation Foundation and its local branches
inner Sydney councils opposed to high-rise development
the Commonwealth to protect heritage buildings in Sydney
the NSW Builders Labourers Federation, led by Jack Mundey
questions.explanation: Builders labourers refused to work on projects that would destroy bushland, heritage areas or working-class housing. Using union power for environmental and community aims was what made the bans new.

questions.stem: Green bans later protected The Rocks and Woolloomooloo as well as bushland. Why do historians see them as a turning point in Australian environmentalism?
options: They were the first time protesters went to the courts to halt city building projects
They led directly to a national ban on the mining of uranium
They showed that unions opposed all new construction in Sydney
They extended environmental concern to urban heritage and communities
questions.explanation: The bans redefined the environment to include the built heritage and the neighbourhoods where people lived, not only wilderness. The union supported building that met community needs; it opposed particular developments, and its weapon was industrial action rather than the courts.

questions.stem: In Commonwealth v Tasmania (1983), the High Court held that the Commonwealth could stop the Franklin Dam. The main constitutional basis was:
options: the trade and commerce power over the interstate sale of Tasmanian hydro-electricity
section 100, which protects the states' reasonable use of river water
the defence power, because the area had strategic military value
the external affairs power, used to carry out the World Heritage Convention
questions.explanation: The Court accepted that the Commonwealth could legislate to meet its obligations under an international treaty, the World Heritage Convention. Section 100 limits Commonwealth trade laws affecting river water and did not give the power to stop the dam.

questions.stem: Peter Dombrovskis's photograph 'Morning Mist, Rock Island Bend' became significant in 1983 because it was:
options: tendered as the key evidence in the High Court Franklin case
adopted as the emblem of the Hydro-Electric Commission
published to attract tourists to the new Lake Pedder
used in advertisements urging voters to save the Franklin River
questions.explanation: During the 1983 federal election campaign, newspaper advertisements used the photograph to ask whether voters could support a party that would destroy the river. It shows how images shaped public opinion about wilderness.

questions.stem: The dispute over sand mining on Fraser Island (K'gari), led by John Sinclair and others, ended in 1976 when the Commonwealth:
options: refused export licences for the island's mineral sands
nationalised the companies that held the mining leases
placed the island on the World Heritage List
returned ownership of the island to the Butchulla people
questions.explanation: After an environmental inquiry, the Fraser government stopped the export of mineral sands from the island, which ended mining. World Heritage listing came in 1992, and Butchulla native title was recognised much later.

questions.stem: Between 1956 and 1963, Maralinga in South Australia was used by:
options: the United States to test long-range missiles over the Nullarbor
Australia to test atomic bombs it had developed for its own defence
France to test hydrogen bombs before moving its tests to the Pacific
Britain to test atomic weapons, with Australian government agreement
questions.explanation: The Menzies government agreed to British atomic tests at Maralinga, following earlier tests at the Monte Bello Islands and Emu Field. Australia never developed its own bombs, and France tested in French Polynesia.

questions.stem: Which statement about the effects of the British atomic tests on Anangu people is accurate?
options: Many were moved off their land, and contamination kept them from returning for decades
They were fully consulted by both governments and gave their consent before testing began
Their land was cleaned up and returned to them before the testing ended in 1963
They were not affected because the area had no Aboriginal people living on it
questions.explanation: Anangu were moved away from the test area and many were exposed to fallout, while plutonium contamination made their land unsafe for decades. Authorities had treated the area as if it were empty, and the land was returned to its owners only in stages from 1984.

questions.stem: The Royal Commission into British Nuclear Tests in Australia (1984–85) is a valuable source for historians mainly because it:
options: was set up by the British government in order to justify the testing program it had run
was carried out while the main atomic tests were still under way
found that the safety measures at the test sites had been adequate
took evidence from Aboriginal witnesses and veterans about the tests' effects
questions.explanation: The Australian commission heard testimony from Aboriginal people and service personnel and was strongly critical of how safety and Aboriginal welfare were handled. It recommended clean-up of the sites. Its distance from the events, three decades later, is also a limitation to weigh.

questions.stem: In 1973 Australia and New Zealand took France to the International Court of Justice over:
options: the bombing of the ship Rainbow Warrior
French mining claims in Antarctica
atmospheric nuclear tests in French Polynesia
French whaling in the Southern Ocean
questions.explanation: The two countries argued that radioactive fallout from France's atmospheric tests in the Pacific endangered them; France moved to underground testing in the mid-1970s. The Rainbow Warrior was sunk by French agents in Auckland in 1985.

questions.stem: The Treaty of Rarotonga, signed in 1985 by Australia and other South Pacific Forum members, established:
options: a ban on uranium mining in Australia
a shared Pacific fisheries authority
joint protection of the Great Barrier Reef
a South Pacific nuclear-free zone
questions.explanation: The treaty banned the testing, manufacture and stationing of nuclear weapons in the zone. It reflected regional anger at French testing, but it did not stop Australia mining or exporting uranium.

questions.stem: How did the 1986 Chernobyl disaster affect debate about nuclear power in Australia?
options: It strengthened anti-nuclear arguments about the dangers of reactors
It led Australia to build a nuclear power station with stricter safety
It ended uranium mining in Australia within the following year
It had no effect because Australia already banned uranium exports
questions.explanation: Chernobyl gave anti-nuclear campaigners vivid evidence of the risks of nuclear power and the spread of fallout across borders. Australia did not build a power reactor, and uranium mining and exports continued.

questions.stem: In 1984 the Nuclear Disarmament Party won a Senate seat for:
options: Peter Garrett in New South Wales
Bob Brown in Tasmania
Judith Wright in Queensland
Jo Vallentine in Western Australia
questions.explanation: The party, formed in 1984, won a Senate seat for Jo Vallentine in Western Australia. Peter Garrett ran as a high-profile candidate in New South Wales but was not elected.

questions.stem: In 1963 Yolngu people at Yirrkala sent bark petitions to the federal parliament. They protested against:
options: the excision of their land for a bauxite mine without consultation
British atomic tests carried out on their land in Arnhem Land
a uranium mine planned on their land inside what later became Kakadu National Park
the flooding of their land for a hydro-electric power scheme
questions.explanation: The petitions, framed with painted designs showing Yolngu law and land, objected to land being taken for bauxite mining on the Gove Peninsula without consulting its owners. They are a landmark in Aboriginal advocacy over mining.

questions.stem: In 1980 the Western Australian Government sent a drilling rig in a police-escorted convoy to Noonkanbah station. The Yungngora community opposed the drilling because:
options: they wanted a larger share of the oil royalties
it would flood the station's irrigated paddocks
the company was really planning a uranium mine
it threatened a sacred site on their land
questions.explanation: The Yungngora people held the station lease and objected that drilling would damage a site of great spiritual significance. The government pushed the drilling through; no oil was found, but the dispute drew national attention to mining on Aboriginal land.

questions.stem: The Ranger Uranium Environmental Inquiry (1975–77), chaired by Justice Fox, recommended that:
options: nuclear power stations should be built near Darwin to use the uranium
mining could go ahead under strict controls, alongside a national park and land rights
uranium mining should be banned permanently throughout the whole of the Northern Territory
the land should be sold outright to the mining company with no conditions
questions.explanation: The Fox Inquiry accepted mining under tight regulation, while recommending a national park and the grant of Aboriginal land in the region, which led towards Kakadu National Park. It did not recommend a ban or nuclear power stations.

questions.stem: The Jabiluka uranium mine, approved in the late 1990s, was never developed. Which factor was most significant?
options: Sustained opposition led by Mirarr Senior Traditional Owner Yvonne Margarula
A High Court ruling that uranium mining in national parks was unconstitutional
A Commonwealth ban on all uranium mining announced in the late 1990s
Discovery that the ore at the site was too low-grade to mine
questions.explanation: The Mirarr, supported by a national blockade in 1998 and international campaigning, refused consent, and the mine was later placed under an agreement not to proceed without their approval. There was no High Court ruling or national ban, and Jabiluka holds high-grade ore.

questions.stem: In 1985 the title to Uluru–Kata Tjuta National Park was handed back to its Anangu owners, who leased it back to be run under:
options: the Australian Conservation Foundation
joint management by Anangu and the national parks agency
sole management by the Northern Territory Government
a mining company holding exploration rights
questions.explanation: The handback made Anangu the owners, with a board that has a majority of Traditional Owners managing the park jointly with the Commonwealth parks agency. Joint management brought Anangu law and knowledge into how the park is cared for.

questions.stem: From the late 1990s the Commonwealth funded Indigenous Protected Areas, and later Indigenous ranger programs. This development best reflects:
options: a return to the colonial doctrine of improvement through clearing and fencing land
the transfer of every national park in Australia to state control
the belief that conservation required removing people from the land
growing acceptance of Indigenous custodianship as a model for conservation
questions.explanation: These programs recognised that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people caring for Country achieve conservation goals. They reject the older idea of 'wilderness' as land without people, which is the most tempting misreading.

questions.stem: The West Arnhem Land Fire Abatement project, begun in 2006, is significant because it:
options: used Aboriginal early dry-season burning to cut greenhouse emissions
banned all burning in Arnhem Land to protect its threatened native wildlife
replaced cultural burning with aerial firefighting from Darwin
created the first national park in the Northern Territory
questions.explanation: Traditional Owners and rangers lit cooler fires early in the dry season, reducing the large late-season wildfires that release more greenhouse gas. Industry paid for the emission reductions, showing old knowledge being valued in a modern economy.

questions.stem: In 2007 the United Nations General Assembly adopted the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, including rights to lands and resources. Australia's response was to:
options: endorse it in 2007 as one of its first supporters
vote against it, then formally endorse it in 2009
vote for it and immediately make it Australian law
abstain from the vote and never endorse it
questions.explanation: Australia was one of four countries, with Canada, New Zealand and the United States, to vote against the Declaration in 2007. The next government endorsed it in 2009, but it is not binding Australian law.

questions.stem: Rachel Carson's Silent Spring (1962) warned that:
options: the world's oil supplies would run out before the year 2000
synthetic pesticides such as DDT were harming wildlife and people
nuclear tests were causing the world's climate to cool rapidly
population growth would soon cause mass famine across Asia
questions.explanation: Carson showed how pesticides moved through food chains, killing birds and other wildlife, and imagined a spring without birdsong. The famine warning belongs to Paul Ehrlich's The Population Bomb (1968).

questions.stem: The poet Judith Wright was a leading figure in the campaign to:
options: end British atomic testing at Maralinga and the Monte Bello Islands
save Kelly's Bush in Hunters Hill from housing development
protect the Great Barrier Reef from oil drilling and limestone mining
stop the flooding of Lake Pedder through the Builders Labourers' bans
questions.explanation: Wright helped found the Wildlife Preservation Society of Queensland and led the 'Save the Reef' campaign of the late 1960s and 1970s. She also supported Aboriginal land rights and a treaty, linking conservation with justice for First Nations people.

questions.stem: The 1987 Brundtland Report, Our Common Future, popularised the idea of:
options: development that meets present needs without harming future generations
deep ecology, which values nature regardless of its usefulness to people
the Anthropocene as a new epoch in the geological history of the Earth
limits to growth, with a call to halt all economic growth by 2000
questions.explanation: The report defined sustainable development as meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs. Deep ecology came from Arne Naess, and The Limits to Growth was a 1972 report for the Club of Rome.

questions.stem: The term 'Anthropocene', popularised by the scientist Paul Crutzen from 2000, refers to:
options: the era of Aboriginal fire management that ended in 1788
a proposed epoch in which human activity shapes Earth's systems
the period when people first arrived on the Australian continent
the age of the giant megafauna before humans reached Australia
questions.explanation: Crutzen argued that human activity had become a force altering the climate, atmosphere and ecosystems on a geological scale, so a new epoch should follow the Holocene. Whether and when it began remains debated.

questions.stem: Some scholars propose that the Anthropocene began with the mid-20th-century 'Great Acceleration'. A key physical marker cited for this date is:
options: the ash layer left by the eruption of Krakatoa in 1883
the warming that ended the last ice age and began the Holocene
pollen from the first crops grown about 10,000 years ago
radioactive fallout from nuclear tests, found in sediments and ice
questions.explanation: Fallout from atmospheric nuclear testing from the early 1950s left a sharp, worldwide signal in layers of sediment and ice. The end of the last ice age marks the start of the Holocene, the epoch the Anthropocene would follow.

questions.stem: Which argument would a critic of the Anthropocene concept most likely make?
options: The Holocene ended when Aboriginal people first arrived in Australia
Geological epochs may not be named after any living species
It blames humanity as a whole for changes driven mostly by industrial nations
Humans have had no measurable effect at all on the Earth's climate or its ecosystems
questions.explanation: Many critics accept that humans have changed the planet but object that the name spreads responsibility evenly, when industrial economies caused most of the change. Indigenous critics add that colonised peoples bore the costs rather than causing them.

questions.stem: The Green Revolution of the 1950s to 1970s increased world food output mainly through:
options: replacing grain crops with large-scale livestock grazing
high-yield crop varieties, fertilisers, pesticides and irrigation
a return to traditional mixed farming without chemical inputs
bans on chemical fertilisers in developing countries
questions.explanation: New varieties of wheat and rice, supported by fertilisers, pesticides and irrigation, greatly increased yields. Critics later pointed to soil damage, chemical pollution and water use, linking the Green Revolution to debates sparked by Silent Spring.

questions.stem: Why did the Pilbara iron ore boom begin in the 1960s?
options: The Commonwealth lifted its embargo on iron ore exports in 1960
Gold deposits in the Pilbara had been worked out by the 1950s
Britain paid for new Australian mines as war reparations
The Snowy Mountains Scheme supplied power to the Pilbara
questions.explanation: An export ban imposed in 1938 had kept the Pilbara's ore untapped; once it was lifted, huge mines, railways and ports were built to supply Japan. The boom made mining central to the economy and raised new questions about mining on Aboriginal land.

questions.stem: Post-war suburban growth in Australian cities contributed to environmental concern mainly by:
options: spreading car-dependent housing over bushland and farmland
crowding most residents into high-rise towers in the centre
reducing each household's use of water and electricity
ending the clearing of native vegetation around cities
questions.explanation: Rapid population growth and rising car ownership pushed low-density suburbs outwards, clearing bush and farmland and increasing consumption of water and energy. These pressures helped build support for conservation from the 1960s.

questions.stem: During the Franklin blockade, protesters were trained in non-violent action and accepted arrest. Critics of the blockade argued that:
options: breaking the law undermined a dam approved by an elected parliament
all protests on public land were forbidden under Australian law
non-violent action was too extreme a method for a democracy
the dam site lay outside Tasmania, so Tasmanians had no say
questions.explanation: Supporters of the dam, including the Tasmanian Government, said decisions should be made by elected parliaments, not by protesters breaking the law. Defenders of direct action replied that peaceful civil disobedience was a legitimate democratic tradition.

questions.stem: Landcare, launched nationally in 1989, is notable because it brought together:
options: the National Farmers' Federation and the Australian Conservation Foundation
the Builders Labourers Federation and the Wilderness Society's Franklin campaigners
the United Tasmania Group and Tasmania's Hydro-Electric Commission
the major mining companies and the Nuclear Disarmament Party
questions.explanation: Landcare grew from an alliance between farmers' and conservation groups, backed by the Hawke government, to repair degraded land through local community groups. It showed environmental concern moving into mainstream rural life.

questions.stem: The Australian Greens were formed as a national party in:
questions.explanation: State green parties joined to form the Australian Greens in 1992. In 1972 the United Tasmania Group formed, and 1983 was the year of the Franklin decision.

questions.stem: Australia's first World Heritage listings, in 1981, were the Great Barrier Reef, Kakadu National Park and:
options: Uluru–Kata Tjuta National Park
the Budj Bim Cultural Landscape
the Willandra Lakes Region
the Tasmanian Wilderness
questions.explanation: The Willandra Lakes in south-western New South Wales were listed for their record of ancient human occupation, including Mungo. The Tasmanian Wilderness was listed in 1982, Uluru in 1987 and Budj Bim in 2019.

questions.stem: Under the 1971 Ramsar Convention on wetlands, Australia designated the world's first wetland of international importance, in 1974, at:
options: Cobourg Peninsula
the Coorong
Kakadu
the Macquarie Marshes
questions.explanation: Cobourg Peninsula in the Northern Territory was the first site listed anywhere under the Ramsar Convention. The early listing shows Australia's growing involvement in international environmental agreements.

questions.stem: Which statement about Australia and the 1997 Kyoto Protocol is accurate?
options: Australia agreed to deeper emission cuts than any other country
Australia signed it but did not ratify it until December 2007
Australia refused to send a delegation to the Kyoto conference
Australia ratified it in 1998, the year after the conference
questions.explanation: Australia negotiated a target allowing its emissions to rise above 1990 levels, signed in 1998 and then declined to ratify. The incoming Rudd government ratified the Protocol in December 2007.

questions.stem: Which government response to the Millennium Drought (about 1996–2010) changed how the Murray–Darling Basin was managed?
options: The Water Act 2007, which created a single Basin authority
The Snowy Mountains Scheme, which diverted rivers inland
The River Murray Waters Agreement between the states
The Irrigation Act, which vested river water in the Crown
questions.explanation: The drought exposed over-allocation of water, and the Water Act 2007 set up the Murray–Darling Basin Authority to plan for the basin as a whole. The other options are much earlier measures: the 1880s, the 1910s and the Snowy scheme begun in 1949.

questions.stem: Which evidence best supports the argument that environmental protest often had limited impact on government decisions?
options: The Little Desert was not subdivided for new farms
Lake Pedder was flooded despite a long national campaign
The Franklin Dam was never built after the 1983 ruling
Green bans saved much of The Rocks from redevelopment
questions.explanation: Lake Pedder is the clearest case of a campaign that failed: the Hydro-Electric Commission completed the scheme in 1972. The other three options are campaigns that succeeded, so they support the opposite argument.

questions.stem: Which example best shows Australian environmentalism shaping global policy rather than only following it?
options: Australian activists took up Rachel Carson's arguments about pesticides in the 1960s
Greenpeace, founded in Canada in 1971, later opened Australian offices
Australia joined the Kyoto Protocol a decade after it was negotiated
Australia and France led the move in 1989 to block mining in Antarctica
questions.explanation: In 1989 the Hawke government, with France, refused to sign a convention that would have allowed regulated Antarctic mining, which led to the 1991 Madrid Protocol banning it. The other options show Australia adopting ideas or agreements that began elsewhere.

questions.stem: Which development best shows continuity between pre-colonial and late 20th-century land management in Australia?
options: The renewed use of Aboriginal cultural burning in parks and ranger programs
The flooding of Lake Pedder to supply hydro-electric power to Tasmanian industry
Large-scale land clearing for wheat during the Green Revolution
The British atomic tests at Maralinga on Anangu land
questions.explanation: Cultural burning by Traditional Owners links practices tens of thousands of years old to modern fire and conservation management. The other options are examples of change that disrupted custodianship of Country.

questions.stem: A historian argues that the deepest change in attitudes to the environment between 1901 and 2010 was a shift from 'improvement' to 'protection'. Which evidence best supports this argument?
options: Drought remained a recurring challenge for farmers throughout the century
Mining continued to drive much of Australia's export growth after 1960
Aboriginal people continued to resist the taking of their land
Governments that once required land clearing came to fund conservation
questions.explanation: Selection laws had made clearing a condition of holding land; by the late 20th century governments funded Landcare, national parks and heritage listing. The other options describe continuities, not a change in attitudes.
